SLOOS-informed adjustment:
- The latest SLOOS (mid-2020) indicates broad-based tightening of lending standards and terms across C&I loans (to firms of all sizes), CRE loans, and consumer credit (credit cards, autos, other consumer), with banks citing a weaker economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, and sector-specific stress. Loan demand from businesses and for CRE declined. Residential mortgage demand (especially refinancing, and some purchase) picked up on low rates, but banks still tightened standards for most mortgage categories.
- These findings imply that, despite improved market functioning from the Fed’s facilities and asset purchases, bank-intermediated credit supply is constrained and could blunt the transmission of easier financial conditions to the real economy. This reinforces the FOMC’s “considerable risks” language on growth, employment, and inflation.
- Policy stance (ELB, strong forward guidance, Treasury and agency MBS/CMBS purchases, repo and ON RRP operations) remains appropriate and supportive, but SLOOS shows meaningful headwinds in credit availability that tilt the outlook more negative than an FSR-only read. Some offset comes from strong mortgage/refi demand.

Net tone: Negative with policy mitigation; SLOOS tightening warrants a more negative tilt than before.
